Chapter 8
Fat—The Right Kind for Your Sports Diet
Eat fat, get fat. Eat fat, clog your arteries. Eat fat, have a heart attack. Eat fat, run
slow. I’m sure you’ve heard this anti-fat chatter. While there is an element of truth
in some of these statements, there is also room for more education. Let’s take a
look at the whole picture.

While dietary fat used to be considered bad, we now know that all fats are not
created equal. The hard, saturated fat in beef, butter and cheese is the “bad” fat,
as is the trans- (partially hydrogenated) fat in commercially baked goods. The
soft, liquid polyunsaturated and monounsaturated fats in fish, olives, peanut
butter, and nuts are the “good” fats, essential for overall good health. Hence,
there’s no need to avoid all fat like the plague.
Olive oil, for example, is health-protective; it is the foundation of the acclaimed
heart-healthy Mediterranean Diet. For centuries, native Italians and Greeks have
enjoyed good health and a 40-percent-fat diet. In general, I recommend that
healthy runners target a sports diet with about 25 percent of the calories from
(primarily healthful) fat. 
How does 25 percent fat translate into food? Let’s say you have 1,800 calories a
day in your calorie budget (this would be a reducing diet for most female runners): 
.25 x 1,800 total calories = 450 calories a day of fat. 
Because there are 9 calories per gram of fat, divide 450 calories by 9:
450 calories / 9 calories per gram = 50 grams of fat in your daily fat budget. 
A 25-percent-fat diet includes a reasonable amount of fat and lets you enjoy a
little fat at each meal.
